column2: >The formula for a random int in [low, high]: (int)(Math.random() * (high - low + 1)) + low
>I: CORRECT. Math.random() * 8 gives [0.0, 8.0). Cast to int gives 0-7. Add 5 gives 5-12.
>II: INCORRECT. Math.random() * 7 gives [0.0, 7.0). Cast to int gives 0-6. Add 5 gives 5-11. It never produces 12.

>III: CORRECT. The + 5 sits inside the cast here, so the shift happens before the truncation rather than after. Math.random() * 8 + 5 gives [5.0, 13.0), and truncating that gives 5 through 12. Adding a whole number before truncating lands on the same integer as adding it after, so III produces the same 5 through 12 that I does.

column1: After ONE pass of selection sort, what is the array?

Selection sort scans the whole unsorted part of the array for the smallest value and swaps it to the front. On the first pass the smallest value is 1, sitting at index 3, so 1 and 5 trade places. Nothing else moves, which leaves [1, 2, 8, 5, 9].
Assuming one pass sorts more than one element into place. [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] is where selection sort finishes, not where it is after a single pass.
Selection sort settles exactly one position per pass. After k passes the first k entries are final and the rest of the array is untouched, so you can answer these without tracing the inner loop.

column2: >I: 14 / 4 + 14 % 4 = 3 + 2 = 5, and 5 == 14 is false. Statement I says it is false, so statement I is correct. Watch the shape of it: the identity that rebuilds x is (x / y) * y + x % y, with the multiply. Drop the multiply and you are left with 3 + 2.
>II: (double) 14 / 4 = 14.0 / 4 = 3.5. 3.5 == 3.5 is true. Statement says this is true. CORRECT.
>III: 14 / 4 * 4 = 3 * 4 = 12. 12 == 14 is false. Statement says this is false. CORRECT.
